prize_parts.citation: For developing methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets from market data.

statement.case_for: I moved my preferred configuration from B025, my opening first choice, to B005 after reading the openings. The case for B005 is that it is a new way of measuring. Random-coefficients demand estimation with endogenous prices lets researchers recover substitution patterns, market power and welfare from market data, which could not be done credibly before. It changed what we know and how we know it. It also reaches well beyond industrial organisation, into merger review, trade, health and environmental policy evaluation. The attribution is the cleanest of the large candidates: the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes demand framework is a coherent three-person unit, and Pakes also anchors the dynamic-industry and estimation strand. The work dates from the 1990s, so it has had decades of use, replication and refinement and there is no timing concern. This fits the criterion I weight most heavily, that a contribution should combine new measurement with lasting use, and the criterion is applied the same way across fields.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the credited list has seven names and any three-person cut excludes people with real claims, notably Bresnahan and Reiss for the earlier new empirical IO tradition, and Benkard and Levin for dynamic models. The contribution can also be read as a toolkit, not a single substantive discovery. Structural estimates remain sensitive to functional-form, instrument and equilibrium assumptions. If the committee thinks the prize should reward a finding about the economy more than a method, B005 is weaker than B025 or B036 on that dimension.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B005 first and proposes Pakes, Berry and Bresnahan. He argues that the breadth of use beyond IO is the main basis for the ranking, and he treats Bresnahan's market-power inference tradition as part of the core. He flags that Levinsohn risks being left out.
responses.response: I agree that breadth of use is the right common criterion, and I note that he states his own IO background as a possible bias. I come out differently on the third name. The prize rationale is demand estimation with endogenous prices, and that is a joint Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes contribution. Bresnahan's earlier work on inferring market power is important, but it is a different contribution. Replacing Levinsohn with Bresnahan would give a citation that mixes two strands and leaves the BLP paper's third author uncredited. I would accept Bresnahan only if the committee chose a deliberately broader empirical-IO citation, and that would need a different citation text.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B005 first. He values the combination of theory, estimation and practical use in antitrust and regulatory work. He also names the concern that this is a methods prize without a single headline substantive finding, and asks whether Bresnahan or Reiss should be preferred to Levinsohn.
responses.response: I take the methods concern seriously, and it is the main reason I do not treat B005 as obviously decisive. My answer is that measurement tools can count as discoveries when they change what can be known. Here the tools made market power, substitution patterns and merger effects measurable with real data, which is close in spirit to how historical national accounts changed the study of long-run growth. I do not agree that the third name should shift to Bresnahan or Reiss, for the attribution reasons I gave above. I accept that this is a judgement call and that the committee could reasonably weigh it differently.

responses.point: Boppart ranks the heterogeneous-firm trade candidate (B025) fifth. He stresses that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum (2003) is an important parallel contribution that is not credited on the ballot, and that Krugman's 2008 prize partly covers adjacent trade theory. He ranks B005 eighth, on diffuse attribution and sensitivity of estimates to implementation.
responses.response: His point about Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is the argument that moved me. I had named it as an uncertainty in my opening but underweighted it. A Melitz-Helpman prize would credit the framework while leaving out a close parallel contribution that other members also flag, and I cannot resolve that from the list text. The B005 attribution problem is real, but it is mostly about which people beyond a clear core to exclude, and the core itself is not contested. I disagree with his low ranking of B005, because implementation sensitivity is a limitation on how the estimates are used, not on the originality of the method. I keep B025 as an alternative because the foundational economics is strong.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer a broader empirical-IO citation that includes Bresnahan or Reiss, and how that would change the three-person limit.
Whether a methods-centred prize is judged to meet the bar against more substantive candidates such as the heterogeneous-firm trade framework (B025) or the New Keynesian framework (B036).

I cannot settle the weight of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum relative to Melitz and Helpman from the list text, and I have not checked independently how recently trade or industrial organisation has been recognised.
I have not independently verified identification or robustness debates about structural demand estimates beyond what the openings state.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for any shortlisted candidate or credited name. My profile shows institutional proximity to colleagues, in that Tommy Andersson is a Lund colleague on the committee and Jan Teorell was formerly at Lund. It shows no connection to the credited names on B005, B025 or B036. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it.
